entries.description: Peak speed of the device's matrix engine (its tensor cores) on full 32-bit numbers. These units multiply whole small blocks of numbers in one step instead of one value at a time.
entries.reason: No fp32xfp32+fp32 coopmat property! Skipped

entries.description: The matrix engine on 16-bit inputs with a 32-bit running total -- the everyday precision of AI inference, and the widest-supported row here. Keeping the total at 32 bits costs accuracy nothing and, on consumer graphics cards, costs half the speed: see the 16-bit-total row below.
entries.reason: No fp16xfp16+fp32 coopmat support (shaderFloat16 or property)! Skipped

entries.description: The matrix engine on 16-bit inputs with the running total also kept at 16 bits. Consumer graphics cards run this at twice the rate of the 32-bit total above, which is why a card's headline AI figure is usually this one; server parts run both alike.
entries.reason: No fp16xfp16+fp16 coopmat support (shaderFloat16 or property)! Skipped

entries.description: The matrix engine on bfloat16 -- 16 bits arranged for AI work, trading digits of accuracy for the number range of a full float, which makes training far more forgiving.
entries.reason: No bf16xbf16+fp32 coopmat support (shaderBFloat16Type or property)! Skipped

entries.description: The matrix engine on 8-bit numbers, in the variant that spends its bits on accuracy rather than range. Half the data of fp16 per value, so the newest hardware runs it at roughly twice the rate.
entries.reason: No fp8-E4M3 coopmat support (VK_EXT_shader_float8 or property)! Skipped

entries.description: The same 8-bit matrix path in the other variant, which spends its bits on range rather than accuracy -- the one that copes with very large and very small values.
entries.reason: No fp8-E5M2 coopmat support (VK_EXT_shader_float8 or property)! Skipped

entries.metric_description: One chain of dot products, each waiting on the one before it.

entries.description: Peak speed of the 8-bit dot-product instruction, which multiplies four pairs of small whole numbers and sums them in one step -- the workhorse of quantized (compressed) neural networks.
entries.metric_description: Two independent chains, so the device has a second dot product to get on with while the first is still finishing.

entries.description: Peak speed of the 8-bit dot-product instruction, which multiplies four pairs of small whole numbers and sums them in one step -- the workhorse of quantized (compressed) neural networks.
entries.metric_description: Four independent chains -- usually enough to keep the dot-product hardware busy with no waiting at all.

entries.description: How many bytes per second the device can stream out of its main memory, reading a buffer far too large to cache. Each reading fetches a different number of values per instruction, since wider fetches usually pull more through before the memory system saturates.
entries.metric_description: One value per thread at a time -- the plain, unvectorised case.

entries.description: How many bytes per second the device moves through shared local memory -- the small on-chip scratchpad a group of threads passes data through, which never goes out to main memory.

entries.description: How many bytes per second the device moves through shared local memory -- the small on-chip scratchpad a group of threads passes data through, which never goes out to main memory.

entries.description: How many bytes per second the device moves through shared local memory -- the small on-chip scratchpad a group of threads passes data through, which never goes out to main memory.
entries.metric_description: Four values per thread at a time, as one 4-wide vector.

entries.description: How many bytes per second the device reads through its texture units, which take a different path to memory than plain buffer reads. Each pixel of the image is read exactly once, so caching cannot flatter the number.
entries.metric_description: Each fetch returns one whole pixel -- four 32-bit colour values, 16 bytes.

entries.description: How fast data crosses between the host's memory and the device's. On a discrete card that means the PCIe link, which is usually far narrower than either side's own memory and is what makes moving data to the device worth avoiding.
entries.metric_description: Host to device: sending data across to the device.

entries.description: How fast data crosses between the host's memory and the device's. On a discrete card that means the PCIe link, which is usually far narrower than either side's own memory and is what makes moving data to the device worth avoiding.
entries.metric_description: Device to host: reading results back. Often slower than the other direction.

entries.description: The overhead of asking the device to do anything at all, measured with a shader that does no work. It is what small, frequent jobs pay before any of their own work begins.
entries.metric_description: One way only: from the moment the host submits the work to the moment the device starts running it.
entries.reason: Needs VK_EXT_calibrated_timestamps

entries.description: The overhead of asking the device to do anything at all, measured with a shader that does no work. It is what small, frequent jobs pay before any of their own work begins.
entries.metric_description: The full round trip -- submit, run, and hear back that it finished. This is what the host waits for if it has nothing else to get on with.
